source_text:
Nam negotii et uisendi mei gratia Romam contenderat, relicta domo, coniuge, liberis, et quod est in liberis amabilius, adhuc annis innocentibus et adhuc dimidiata uerba temptantibus, loquellam ipso offensantis linguae fragmine dulciorem.
quo in aduentu eius non possum exprimere sermonibus, quanto quamque inpatienti gaudio exultauerim, cum augeret maxime laetitiam meam amicissimi hominis inopinata praesentia.
igitur post unum et alterum diem, cum iam et auiditatem desiderii frequens adsiduitatis usus implesset et quae per absentiam mutuam de nobis nesciebamus, relatione alterna comperissemus, placuit Ostiam petere, amoenissimam ciuitatem, quod esset corpori meo siccandis umoribus de marinis lauacris blanda et adposita curatio: sane et ad uindemiam feriae iudiciariam curam relaxauerant. nam id temporis post aestiuam diem in temperiem semet autumnitas dirigebat.
itaque cum diluculo ad mare inambulando litore pergeremus, ut et aura adspirans leniter membra uegetaret et cum eximia uoluptate molli uestigio cedens harena subsideret, Caecilius simulacro Serapidis denotato, ut uulgus superstitiosus solet, manum ori admouens osculum labiis inpressit.
thought_title: Arrival at Ostia and Caecilius kisses an idol
orientation: Marcus the narrator recounts how his friend Octavius came to Rome, and how the three friends went to Ostia, where Caecilius kissed an image of Serapis.
pass_a_gloss: For he had hurried to Rome for the sake of business and of visiting me, having left behind home, wife, children, and—what is more lovable in children—still in innocent years and still attempting half-formed words, a speech sweeter than the very fragment of the stumbling tongue. At his arrival I cannot express in words how much and with how impatient a joy I exulted, since the unexpected presence of a most dear friend increased my happiness especially. Therefore after one day and a second, when now both the frequent practice of constant companionship had filled the eagerness of longing and we had learned by mutual report the things which we did not know about each other through mutual absence, it pleased us to seek Ostia, a most pleasant city, because for my body, for drying the humors, a soothing and suitable cure from the sea baths was available: indeed also for the vintage the holidays had relaxed the judicial business. For at that time after the summer day autumn was directing itself into mildness. And so when at dawn we were proceeding to the sea, walking along the shore, so that both the breeze blowing gently might invigorate our limbs and the sand, yielding to our soft step, might sink down with exceptional pleasure, Caecilius, having noticed an idol of Serapis, as the superstitious crowd is accustomed, moving his hand to his mouth pressed a kiss on his lips.

choices.term: loquellam ipso offensantis linguae fragmine dulciorem
choices.english: a speech sweeter than the very fragment of the stumbling tongue
choices.why: Keeps the literal comparison: the child's half-formed speech is sweeter than the broken sound itself; 'fragment' preserves the physical image of broken syllables.
rejected: babble sweeter than the very stumbling of the tongue
talk sweeter than the broken sound itself

choices.why: The adjective 'inpatienti' modifies 'gaudio' and conveys eager, restless joy; 'impatient' is the literal sense and fits the emotional register.
Both nouns are kept in a genitive chain to preserve the literal force: the eagerness that belongs to longing.
Medical language is retained literally; 'humors' is the standard English for bodily fluids in ancient medicine.
Uses the glossary term 'superstition' in adjectival form; 'crowd' renders the collective singular 'uulgus'.

choices.english: pressed a kiss on his lips
choices.why: Literal rendering of the gesture: he moved his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss onto his lips (i.e., kissed his hand toward the idol).
rejected: imprinted a kiss with his lips
pressed his lips in a kiss

pass_b_english: He had hurried to Rome for business and to see me, leaving behind his home, his wife, his children, and what is more lovable in children: those still in their innocent years, still attempting half-formed words, a speech all the sweeter for its very stammering.
I cannot express in words how great and how impatient a joy I exulted in at his arrival, since the unexpected presence of my dearest friend increased my happiness above all.

And so after a day or two, when frequent time together had filled the eagerness of longing and we had learned through mutual report what we had not known about each other during our absence, we decided to seek Ostia, a most pleasant city, because it offered my body a soothing and suitable cure for drying the humors through sea baths; and indeed the judicial holiday had relaxed my professional cares for the vintage season. For at that time of year, after the summer heat, autumn was turning toward mildness.

And so when at dawn we were making our way to the sea, walking along the shore so that the gently breathing breeze might refresh our limbs and the yielding sand sink softly under our steps with exquisite pleasure, Caecilius noticed an idol of Serapis and, as the superstitious crowd is accustomed to do, moved his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss with his lips.

problems.quote: a speech sweeter than the very fragment of the stumbling tongue
problems.source_quote: loquellam ipso offensantis linguae fragmine dulciorem
problems.why: Latin comparative 'dulciorem' modifies 'loquellam,' not 'fragmine'—the speech is sweeter, not the fragment. Misread syntax.
problems.fix: a speech sweeter for the very stumbling fragment of the tongue
problems.ruling: Latin 'offensantis linguae' = 'offending tongue', not 'stumbling tongue'; mis‑translation alters meaning.

problems.quote: moved his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss on his lips
problems.source_quote: manum ori admouens osculum labiis inpressit
problems.why: 'labiis' is ambiguous but context and 'ori admouens' show he kissed his own hand/lips to the idol, not 'his lips' as idol's. 'Labiis' likely his own lips or hand to lips. English implies idol has lips.
problems.fix: pressed a kiss with his lips to his hand
problems.ruling: 'manum ori admouens' = hand to the idol's mouth; 'osculum labiis inpressit' = kiss on its lips, not his own.

edits.old: a speech sweeter than the very fragment of the stumbling tongue
edits.new: a speech sweeter for the very fragment of the stumbling tongue

edits.old: moved his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss on his lips
edits.new: moved his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss with his lips

fixed: Corrected 'a speech sweeter than the very fragment of the stumbling tongue' to 'a speech sweeter for the very fragment of the stumbling tongue': Latin 'loquellam ipso offensantis linguae fragmine dulciorem' has 'dulciorem' modifying 'loquellam', with 'ipso...fragmine' as ablative of cause, so the speech is sweeter because of the fragment, not sweeter than it.

Corrected 'moved his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss on his lips' to 'moved his hand to his mouth and pressed a kiss with his lips': Latin 'manum ori admouens osculum labiis inpressit' describes Caecilius kissing his own hand, with 'labiis' as instrumental ablative, not the idol's lips.

problems.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
problems.why: Octavius suddenly calls Caecilius 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks it's a new person.
problems.fix: Add note that Natalis is Caecilius's cognomen.

problems.quote: what is more lovable in children: those still in their innocent years, still attempting half-formed words, a speech sweeter for the very fragment of the stumbling tongue
problems.why: Awkward construction; 'a speech sweeter for the very fragment' is unclear—does 'fragment' mean 'stammering'?
problems.fix: 'a speech all the sweeter for its very stammering'

edits.old: what is more lovable in children: those still in their innocent years, still attempting half-formed words, a speech sweeter for the very fragment of the stumbling tongue.
edits.new: what is more lovable in children: those still in their innocent years, still attempting half-formed words, a speech all the sweeter for its very stammering.

fixed: The 'Natalis' problem is not present in this section; no edit needed.

The awkward construction is real: the source 'loquellam ipso offensantis linguae fragmine dulciorem' means the speech is sweeter because of the very stammering, so I clarified it as 'a speech all the sweeter for its very stammering.'

polish.changed: Clarified the narrator's friend as Caecilius, removed the intrusive dash, and smoothed sentence rhythm while preserving every detail and qualification.

notes.why: The pagan opponent is called Caecilius in most sections but addressed as Marcus in others, confusing the reader about identity.
notes.fix: Standardize the name to Caecilius or explain that Marcus is his praenomen.

notes.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
notes.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.
